transcript: Chapter 12. Mrs. Lask told him that visiting was in the afternoons. She told him at the eleventh hour of the night, standing behind a desk inside the doors of a long, low building with a turf roof, and she told him without one grain of malice, the way you tell somebody which way the road goes. She was about fifty, and she had a cardigan in the list. Who do I talk to? said Jab, Dr. Sowerby. When? When? Not tonight. He's in with your brother now, and he'll be in with him a while. Then who else? Mrs. Lask looked at him. There isn't an else, she said. Then I'll wait for him. Visiting, said Mrs. Lask, is in the afternoons. I know, said Jab. Who do I talk to about waiting? It went on like that for a while. He was not rude, and he did not raise his voice, and he had nothing whatever to threaten anybody with, and he had discovered at some point around the third exchange that the only currency he had left in the world was that he was still standing there. At the twelfth hour, Mrs. Lask put down her pen. There's a bench outside the doors, she said. I'm told it's very cold. All right. And there's one inside them, along that wall, which is for people waiting to be sent for. She wrote something on her list without looking up. I haven't sent for you. I don't want you thinking I have. Jab sat down on the bench inside the doors. It was warm. There were pipes behind it. He sat there in his socks with a paper band on his wrist and his collar open, and he did not sleep. And at some point in the small hours, a young woman in white came along the corridor with a tray and stopped in front of him and said, Right. Arm. In a voice that expected no discussion, and cut the field dressing off his forearm and cleaned out the hole in it and put eleven stitches in it while he watched. That's a bite, she said. Yes. What bit you? A hound. When? About the sixth hour. She stopped what she was doing and looked at him properly for the first time. You've been sitting on this bench for six hours with a hound bite, she said. I've been waiting to be sent for, said Jab. Dr. Sowerby came out at the eighth hour with a folder under his arm and found him on the bench. He was small and bald and in a hurry. And he was in a hurry in a way Jab recognized instantly and trusted immediately because it was the way his father's aunt had been in a hurry. A man moving fast because there was a great deal to do and none of it was going to be done by standing still and being kind about it. He did not sit down. You're the brother. Yes. Right, said Dr. Sowerby. I do this in the order I always do it in, which is the bad thing, then the good thing, then the bill, and I've been told I do it too fast, so stop me whenever you like and I won't mind. Is he alive? Dr. Sowerby stopped. Yes, he said. I should have started there and I didn't, and that's the second time this month. And you may take it as read for the rest of this conversation that if anything of that kind changes, I will say it before anything else. He put the folder down on the bench and sat on the arm of it, which was as close to sitting down as he apparently came. He's alive. He's warm. He's got fluid in him, and he's got the first of the medicine in him. And he's been asleep since the fourth hour, which is the best thing that's happened to him in a week. Now the bad thing. And there's a lot of it. The break's the least of it. I want you to hear that first, because everybody gets it the wrong way round. The break is bad. It's a bad break in the shinbone. It's shifted. It's been shifted for seven weeks, and it has spent those seven weeks knitting itself into a shape that is not the shape a leg is. If that was the whole of it, I'd have somebody straighten it this morning, and you'd have a cross child in a frame for three months, and I'd be talking to somebody else by now. The trouble is what got in through the skin when it happened. There's an infection in the bone. Not round it. In it. It's been in there the better part of two months, and it has killed a piece of that bone. And the piece is dead. And dead bone doesn't come back and medicine doesn't reach into it. Because there's nothing alive in there for the blood to carry medicine along. It sits in the leg being a place for the infection to live. And it will go on doing that for as long as it's in him. And while it's in him, he will keep having the nights you have been sitting up through, until one of them doesn't stop. Jab sat on the bench with his hands on his knees. How long? He said. How long what? If nobody does anything, how long has he got? I'm not going to guess at that. Guess, said Jab. Dr. Sowerby looked at him for a moment. Weeks, he said. Possibly not many. And I want to say the other half of that. Which is that you got him here at about the last edge of the time in which any of what I'm going to say next is worth saying. And I'm told you did it on your back. And I'd rather say that to your face than have you find out in six months that everybody in this building said it to each other. The good thing, said Dr. Sowerby. Go on. We can take it out. Open the leg. Take out what's dead. Wash out what's left. And get the medicine to the part that's still alive. That's Kiel. She does the bones and she is very much better at it than I am. And she has already looked at him once tonight. And she'll look at a picture of the inside of that leg this morning. And then she'll tell you her own version of all this. And it will be shorter and worse. While she's in there, she'll take the bad union apart and set it straight. And hold it in a frame. Pins through the bone. A bar on the outside. Ugly as anything you've ever seen and better than plaster for a leg with a hole in it. And with those things and about eight weeks of the medicine, that infection goes out of him. Not every time. Most times. I'm not going to give you a fraction because you'll do arithmetic with it. I'd like the fraction, said Jab. I thought you might, said Dr. Sowerby. About four and five for the infection. First time of asking. Of the one and five, most get there at the second operation. A few don't get there at all. And for those, it's the leg. And I'm saying that out loud in this corridor rather than letting you find it under a door at three in the morning. Jab sat with that. Four and five, he said. Four and five. And if I say do it, when? This afternoon, said Dr. Sowerby. Now the bill, said Dr. Sowerby. And I'm going to do the money part in four words. Because it's four words, it doesn't cost anything. His admission's clinical. It went through at the gate. The operation, the frame, the medicine, the bed, the months. And there will be months are not conditional on anything at all. And there is no window in this station at which anybody can put a price on them. And if a person tells you differently, that person is wrong and you are to send them to me. Everybody keeps telling me that, said Jab. Yes, and everybody will go on telling you, because it's true and because nobody believes it until they've been told about nine times. Sowerby picked up his folder. And now the rest of the bill, which is the part I actually meant, because money is the cheapest thing in this conversation. He is going to pay for this leg for the rest of his life. I'll give you the whole of it now and you may tell me to stop. He will be in that frame until the spring. He will not stand on it before then. And he will not walk properly on it for a good while after that. And there's going to be a stretch in the middle where he hates every one of us and you most of all. Because you'll be the one who's there. Then there's the growing. He tapped the side of his own knee. The place a child's leg grows from is up at the top of the shin, just under the knee. And it is a small and stupid and fragile thing. And it is very near where this has been sitting for two months. Kiel will know more when she's in there and I want you to hear this as a likelihood and not a promise. That leg is not going to grow at the same rate as the other one. Which means that at eight he'll be a boy with one leg a little shorter than the other. And at fifteen he'll be a young man with one leg a good deal shorter and somewhere in the middle of that there'll be a built-up boot and probably another operation and possibly two. So. He'll walk. I'd say that with confidence. He'll walk with a limp. And he'll always know the weather in it. And he will not run like other people. And he will find that out at about six. And it will be a bad year. And he'll be coming back through those doors every year until he's done growing. For somebody to measure him. There was a long silence in the corridor of a long, low building at the eighth hour of the morning. Say the last one again, said Jab. Every year until he's done growing. Here. Here, said Dr. Sowerby. There's one machine in the shed at the north end of this station that takes the picture. And there's one keel and I don't know of another of either within four hundred miles. And I've looked. Because I have a woman in that ward who has been asking me to find one for eleven years. He stood up. That's the bill. I'm sorry to hand you it in a corridor. I'd have done it in a room with chairs if there'd been a day for it. And there isn't. Jab sat on the bench and did the arithmetic. Because his head would not do anything else. And had never once in seventeen years done anything else. And had got him and his brother four hundred miles. Thirteen years until Tonk was done growing. Thirteen winters. Thirteen years of being inside a wall that reviewed a household every so often on what it reckoned that household was worth. He had carried his brother out of the home valley to save his life. And he had. And the price was that neither of them was ever going home. Right. He said. I need a yes. Said Dr. Sowerby. For this afternoon. I need it from whoever's the family. And there's a column in this folder. And the woman at the desk says the windows got you down as head of household. I'm seventeen. Yes. There's a man four hundred miles north who'd have argued about it for a week. Said Jab. Is he here? No. Then it's you. Said Dr. Sowerby. Jab looked at the floor of the corridor for a moment. It was poured concrete with a drain. Yes. He said. They let him into the ward at the ninth hour, which was not the afternoon. And nobody explained why. And Mrs. Lask did not look up from her list as he went past. It was a long room with beds down both sides and a window over every bed. And a light in the ceiling that did not flicker. And it smelled of soap and something sharp underneath. His brother was in the fifth bed on the right. In a white gown. In a white bed. Under a window. He was asleep. Somebody had washed him. All of him. His hair, too. Which was lying flat and dark and clean on a pillow instead of standing up in the two directions it had stood up in for six weeks. There was a needle in the back of his hand with a tube going up to a bag on a hook. The leg was out from under the blanket in a padded trough with the wrapping off. And Jab, who had not seen it in a proper light in seven weeks, looked at it for four seconds and then looked at the window. The wooden fish was on the pillow beside his head where somebody had put it. Jab sat down in the chair. Jab sat down in the chair. He put one hand on the bed beside his brother's hand and did not take hold of it. Because the needle was in that one. And he sat there in a warm room in a dry shirt somebody had given him. And after a while his eyes did something and he put his head down on the blanket. You're the brother, said a voice from across the ward. He got his head up. In the bed opposite, under the other window, there was an old woman sitting up against her pillows. She was very thin and very straight, with white hair cut short and a long face that had been out in a great deal of weather. And she had a tray across her lap with a cup on it. And she was looking at him with a pair of pale eyes that did not appear to miss anything. They brought him in at the second hour, she said. I was awake. I'm always awake at the second hour. It's the one thing in this building nobody's managed to do anything about. There was a great deal of running and a boy shouting about a fish. She paused. Nobody runs in here. I'd like that understood. I've been in this room a month and I've seen them run twice and both times it was for a child. He's four, said Jab. I know. He told the entire ward. The old woman picked up her cup. She did it slowly, watching her own hand go round it the whole way. Senna. Jab. Yes, said Senna. I heard that too. I heard that too. You've been told about medicine and residence, she said. A while later, when he had got some of the tea she had made a nurse fetch him and had discovered he could not hold the cup very well. Three times. You'll be told six more. Nobody believes it. I believe it, said Jab. That's not the trouble. No. No. Senna agreed. It never is. She put her cup down and left her hand on it, looking at the hand. I'll tell you mine and then I'll stop. Because I'm not going to be a woman in a bed who tells a boy what to do with his life on the first morning. I came in on a board four weeks ago. There's a machine in a shed at the north end of this place, and it is the only one of its kind anybody here has ever heard of. And I have to be within a mile of it every eleven days for the rest of my life. Eleven days. Not a fortnight if I'm careful. Eleven. My course is clinical. It went through at that gate, and it is owed to nobody, and it is conditional on nothing. And the man at the window made me a promise about it that he did not have to make, and he has kept it. And a man I would have gone into a fire for signed four seasons of the worst work in this station so that I could have an address within a mile of that shed. She said it without any weight on it at all. The way you say a distance. Not my medicine. My address. That's the whole of the trick. And it isn't a lie anywhere in it. And I want to be extremely clear that I am not telling you to do anything. Because you've got a bandage on your arm and a child in that bed and you have been awake for a day and a half.
